title: Issue-Spotting: Negligence (Duty, Breach, Causation, Damages)
prompt: Read the fact pattern and write an IRAC analysis of the negligence issues. Facts: GreenMart, a grocery store, mops its produce aisle at 5:00 p.m. but places no warning sign and leaves the floor visibly wet. At 5:10 p.m., Priya, a shopper looking at overhead price signs, slips on the wet floor and falls, fracturing her wrist. As a stocker rushes over to help, he knocks over a display, and a falling can strikes Priya's ankle, spraining it. Priya also had brittle bones from a prior condition, which made the wrist fracture more severe than it would have been for an average person. Priya sues GreenMart for negligence. Analyze duty, breach, causation (actual and proximate), and damages, and address any defenses. Write a structured IRAC (or multi-issue IRAC) response.
blurb: A negligence fact pattern engineered to test each element — plus the eggshell-plaintiff rule, an intervening cause, and comparative fault.

rubric.label: Issue spotting
rubric.description: Identifies all four negligence elements as distinct issues plus the wrinkles: the eggshell-skull (brittle bones) rule going to extent of damages, the stocker's falling can as an intervening/superseding-cause question, and comparative/contributory negligence (Priya looking up) as a defense.

rubric.label: Rule statement
rubric.description: States each element correctly: duty (reasonable care; special duty of a business/land possessor to an invitee), breach (reasonable-person standard, or Hand formula B<PL), actual cause (but-for / substantial factor), proximate cause (foreseeability/scope of risk), damages (actual harm). States eggshell rule and superseding-cause doctrine.

rubric.label: Application to facts
rubric.description: Applies each rule to specifics: invitee status, the untended wet floor with no sign as breach, but-for causation of the fall, foreseeability of the wrist fracture, and separately analyzes the can/ankle injury and the brittle-bone severity.

rubric.label: Counterarguments & defenses
rubric.description: Argues both sides: GreenMart's comparative-fault argument (Priya distracted, not watching the floor), whether the stocker's clumsiness is a superseding cause cutting off liability for the ankle, and open-and-obvious-danger doctrine.

rubric.label: Conclusion
rubric.description: Reaches a defensible bottom line on likely liability and on which injuries are recoverable (wrist yes, including enhanced severity under eggshell rule; ankle likely yes as foreseeable rescue/response), acknowledging the comparative-fault reduction.

rubric.label: IRAC structure & organization
rubric.description: Clear IRAC (or CRAC) organization; separates the four elements and the sub-issues; signposts; no undifferentiated fact-dump.

rubric.label: Precision & legal writing
rubric.description: Uses terms of art correctly (invitee, breach, but-for cause, proximate cause, superseding cause, eggshell plaintiff, comparative negligence); avoids conclusory leaps.

reference.scenario: Premises-liability slip-and-fall built to exercise every negligence element and three classic doctrines. Priya is a business invitee, so GreenMart owes an affirmative duty to inspect for and warn of/remedy hazards. Mopping and leaving a visibly wet floor with no sign at a busy hour is a strong breach case (cheap precaution — a sign — versus foreseeable falls, i.e., B<PL). But-for and proximate cause of the wrist fracture are clean; the eggshell-skull rule means GreenMart takes Priya as it finds her, so the enhanced severity from brittle bones is fully recoverable. The stocker knocking a can onto her ankle is the interesting proximate-cause wrinkle: a negligent rescue/response to the original hazard is generally foreseeable and within the scope of the risk, so it is NOT a superseding cause — GreenMart likely remains liable for the ankle too. Priya's looking at overhead signs supports a comparative-negligence reduction (and possibly open-and-obvious argument), reducing but not eliminating recovery in a comparative-fault jurisdiction. Strong answers argue both sides on the superseding cause and the open-and-obvious defense.
model_points: Duty: GreenMart is a land possessor and Priya a business invitee; duty to exercise reasonable care, including to inspect for hazards and to warn of or remedy known/discoverable dangers.

Breach: leaving a visibly wet floor with no warning sign at 5 p.m. breaches the standard of reasonable care. Hand formula framing: B (a cheap wet-floor sign) is far less than P x L (probable slip-and-fall injuries), so failure to take the precaution is unreasonable.
Actual cause: but-for the un-signed wet floor, Priya would not have slipped and fractured her wrist. Satisfied.
Proximate cause (wrist): a slip-and-fall is precisely the risk that makes a wet floor negligent; harm is within the scope of the risk and foreseeable. Satisfied.

Eggshell-skull rule: the defendant takes the plaintiff as it finds her; the brittle-bone condition making the fracture worse goes to the extent of damages, not to liability or foreseeability — full enhanced damages recoverable.
The ankle/can injury — actual cause: but-for the fall, the stocker would not have rushed over and knocked the can. Satisfied.

The ankle/can injury — proximate cause / superseding cause: analyze whether the stocker's clumsy response is a superseding intervening cause. Rule: a foreseeable intervening cause does not cut off liability; negligent rescue or response to a hazard the defendant created is generally foreseeable (danger-invites-rescue). Conclusion: not superseding; GreenMart likely liable for the ankle too. Counterargument: an unforeseeable, freakish response could superseded — argue the store's own employee makes it more, not less, foreseeable.
Damages: actual physical harm (fractured wrist + sprained ankle + enhanced severity). Recoverable.

Defense — comparative negligence: Priya was looking at overhead price signs, not the floor. In a comparative-fault jurisdiction this reduces recovery by her share of fault (e.g., pure or modified comparative); in a (rare) contributory-negligence jurisdiction it could bar recovery. Argue reasonableness — shoppers are expected to look at product/price signage.

Defense — open and obvious: GreenMart may argue the wet floor was open and obvious, negating duty to warn; rebut that a distracted shopper's inattention to an obvious hazard is itself foreseeable, so a duty to remedy may remain.
Conclusion: GreenMart is likely liable for negligence; Priya recovers for both injuries and the enhanced fracture severity, subject to a comparative-fault reduction for her inattention.

probes.trigger: candidate discusses breach but skips the invitee/duty basis
probes.question: What is the source and scope of GreenMart's duty here — does Priya's status as a shopper change what the store owed her?

probes.trigger: candidate treats the brittle bones as reducing foreseeability or damages
probes.question: How does the eggshell-skull rule apply to the more-severe fracture — does it affect liability, foreseeability, or only the measure of damages?

probes.trigger: candidate ignores the falling-can/ankle injury or lumps it in
probes.question: Separately analyze the ankle injury: is the stocker knocking over the display a superseding cause that cuts off GreenMart's liability?

probes.trigger: candidate finds full liability with no defense analysis
probes.question: Priya was looking at overhead signs rather than the floor. What defense does that support, and what is its effect on recovery in a comparative-fault state?

probes.trigger: candidate is conclusory on proximate cause
probes.question: State your proximate-cause test precisely and apply it — is the harm within the scope of the risk that made GreenMart's conduct negligent?

red_flags: Conclusory analysis: 'GreenMart was negligent because the floor was wet' with no element-by-element treatment.
Conflates actual cause and proximate cause, or omits one entirely.
Treats the brittle-bone condition as breaking the chain of causation instead of applying the eggshell rule.
Ignores the falling-can/ankle injury or fails to raise the superseding-cause question.
No defense analysis — misses comparative/contributory negligence despite the 'looking up' fact.
States the reasonable-person standard but never applies it to the no-sign facts.
Fact-dump with no rule statements, or rules with no application.
Awards or denies recovery categorically without acknowledging the comparative-fault reduction.
follow_ups: Suppose GreenMart had put out a clearly visible 'Wet Floor' sign and Priya still fell while reading price tags. How does breach and comparative fault shift?
If the jurisdiction follows pure contributory negligence rather than comparative fault, how does the outcome change?
Imagine the falling can had instead struck a different customer standing nearby. Analyze proximate cause as to that third party.
How would res ipsa loquitur, if at all, apply to the wet-floor fall?
reference.exemplar_answer: Issue 1 (Duty): Rule — a land possessor owes a business invitee reasonable care, including to inspect for and warn of or remedy hazards. Application — Priya is a shopper, i.e., an invitee, so GreenMart owed her that affirmative duty. Conclusion — duty established. Issue 2 (Breach): Rule — breach is failing to act as a reasonable person; under the Hand formula, conduct is unreasonable when the burden of precaution (B) is less than probability times loss (P x L). Application — a wet-floor sign is a trivial burden, while the probability and severity of shopper falls on a visibly wet aisle at a busy hour are substantial, so leaving no sign breaches the standard. Conclusion — breach. Issue 3 (Causation — wrist): Actual cause — but-for the unsigned wet floor, Priya would not have slipped; satisfied. Proximate cause — a slip-and-fall is the very risk that makes a wet floor negligent, so the wrist fracture is within the scope of the risk and foreseeable. Eggshell rule — GreenMart takes Priya as it finds her; her brittle bones increase the extent of damages but do not defeat foreseeability or liability, so the enhanced severity is fully recoverable. Issue 4 (Causation — ankle/can): Actual cause — but-for the fall, the stocker would not have rushed and knocked the can; satisfied. Proximate/superseding cause — Rule: a foreseeable intervening cause does not cut off liability, and a negligent response or rescue to a hazard the defendant created is generally foreseeable. Application — the store's own employee responding to the fall makes the mishap foreseeable, not freakish. Counterargument — GreenMart may call it an unforeseeable superseding act, but that is the weaker view. Conclusion — GreenMart remains liable for the ankle. Issue 5 (Damages): fractured wrist (enhanced), sprained ankle — actual physical harm, recoverable. Issue 6 (Defenses): Comparative negligence — Priya was reading overhead signs, not the floor, supporting a fault allocation that reduces her recovery in a comparative-fault jurisdiction (a contributory-negligence state could bar it); rebut that shopper attention to signage is expected. Open-and-obvious — even an obvious wet floor may leave a duty to remedy given foreseeable distraction. Overall conclusion: GreenMart is likely liable in negligence for both injuries, including the enhanced fracture severity under the eggshell rule, with recovery reduced by Priya's comparative share of fault.

interviewer_notes: Written IRAC exercise; the candidate types the analysis. This fact pattern is engineered so a complete answer must (1) march through all four elements as separate issues, (2) apply the eggshell-skull rule to the brittle-bone fact — a common trap where weak candidates wrongly treat it as reducing foreseeability, (3) run a real superseding-cause analysis on the falling can, and (4) raise comparative/contributory negligence off the 'looking at overhead signs' fact. If the candidate collapses duty and breach or skips causation, use the duty and proximate-cause probes to force element-by-element discipline. Reward answers that argue both sides of the superseding-cause and open-and-obvious questions rather than asserting a conclusion. The single most-missed spot is usually the ankle/can injury; if omitted, deploy that probe directly. Strong (senior-leaning) answers frame breach with the Hand formula and note the jurisdictional split on contributory vs. comparative fault.
